qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Identify two distinct expenditure-pattern characteristics in invented monthly budgets: A receives N$3,000, spends N$2,400 on essentials and saves N$150; B receives N$9,000, spends N$4,500 on essentials and saves N$1,800.
items.canonical_answer: A spends a larger income share on essentials, 80% versus 50%. B saves a larger share, 20% versus 5%.
marking_guidance: Characteristic (1): essential share comparison, with numerical example. Distinct feature (1): saving share comparison, with example.
objective_titles: Describe how and why different income groups have different expenditure patterns (spending, saving, borrowing)

items.prompt: Explain why a lower-income household may spend a larger income share on essentials than a higher-income household with similar basic needs.
items.canonical_answer: Basic needs absorb much of the smaller budget. Income can rise faster than the cost of meeting those needs, leaving the higher-income household a larger remainder; its essential share can be lower even if the money amount is higher.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): Essential needs absorb much of the smaller income.
Because/mechanism (1): Larger income can exceed the increase in essential costs.
Mechanism development (1): More remains after necessities at higher income.
Consequence (1): The essential income share can fall even if its cash amount rises.

objective_titles: Explain income-group spending patterns through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain the amount-versus-share comparison where invented A spends N$2,400 of N$3,000 income on essentials and B spends N$4,500 of N$9,000.
items.canonical_answer: B spends more money, N$4,500 versus N$2,400, but a lower income share, 50% versus 80%. A smaller share does not mean a smaller amount.
marking_guidance: Context (1): B spends more cash, N$4,500 versus N$2,400.
Reason/conclusion (1): B spends a lower share, 50% versus 80%, so amount and share differ.

items.prompt: Explain why saving can rise when income increases but essential needs and other commitments rise by less than income.
items.canonical_answer: The increase leaves more income after current commitments. Some of that remainder can be withheld from current consumption and saved, allowing higher saving if the household chooses it; higher capacity does not force that choice.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): Income rises faster than current commitments.
Because/mechanism (1): The remainder after consumption increases.
Mechanism development (1): Part of it can be withheld from present consumption.
Consequence (1): Saving can increase if chosen; greater capacity does not force saving.
items.repair_note: Jeremy-authorised repairs for Claude review 6145-AUTH-R1: terminology, central-bank functions, precise definitions, specific credit points and misconception discrimination.
objective_titles: Explain income-group saving patterns through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why a household with strong precautionary motives may still save little when essentials absorb almost all its income.
items.canonical_answer: The desire for a reserve does not remove the budget constraint. Little income remains to set aside after necessary consumption, so limited saving need not show a weak motive.
marking_guidance: Context (1): Essentials absorb almost all income.
Reason/conclusion (1): Little capacity remains to save despite a strong precautionary motive.

items.prompt: Explain why low income can produce a strong need for emergency borrowing but limited actual credit.
items.canonical_answer: An urgent cost can exceed current funds, creating loan demand. Low remaining income makes repayments difficult and may lead a lender to restrict access. Thus a strong need can coexist with little borrowing.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): An emergency cost exceeds current funds.
Because/mechanism (1): A household therefore wants credit.
Mechanism development (1): Low remaining income makes repayment difficult and may restrict approval.
Consequence (1): Strong credit need can coexist with little actual borrowing.

items.prompt: Explain the affordability problem for a household with N$150 monthly funds remaining and a proposed N$400 monthly repayment, with other conditions unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: The repayment exceeds the available remainder by N$250. Without higher income or reduced spending, the budget cannot accommodate it even if a loan is offered.
marking_guidance: Context (1): N$400 repayment exceeds the N$150 remainder by N$250.
Reason/conclusion (1): The loan is unaffordable on the unchanged budget without an adjustment.

items.prompt: Explain the difference in timing when a household saves towards a later purchase rather than borrowing to buy it immediately.
items.canonical_answer: Saving postpones consumption while funds accumulate, reducing current spending capacity. Borrowing brings the purchase forward but creates future repayments and charges. The choice reallocates resources between present and future periods.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): Saving delays the purchase while funds accumulate.
Because/mechanism (1): This reduces present consumption capacity.
Mechanism development (1): Borrowing brings the purchase forward.
Consequence (1): Repayments and charges reduce later available resources.

items.prompt: Explain the two motives when a household borrows for an urgent roof repair because adequate savings have not yet accumulated.
items.canonical_answer: The spending motive is maintaining shelter now. The borrowing motive is bridging the shortage of present funds so the urgent repair can precede future income.
marking_guidance: Context (1): The spending motive is to maintain shelter through the roof repair.
Reason/conclusion (1): The borrowing motive is to bridge the current funding gap before future income.

items.prompt: Explain why failure of a household’s cooking appliance can change its spending priorities when it needs the appliance for daily meals.
items.canonical_answer: Failure removes a useful household service. Replacing the appliance restores meal preparation, increasing the priority of that purchase and potentially displacing discretionary spending within the budget.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): The failed appliance removes daily cooking service.
Because/mechanism (1): A replacement restores meal preparation.
Mechanism development (1): Restoring that necessary service raises purchase priority.
Consequence (1): The fixed budget may require less discretionary spending.

items.prompt: Explain a spending motive for necessary transport to work when the traveller has no feasible walking alternative.
items.canonical_answer: The journey enables attendance at work, meeting a practical need. The spending motive follows from necessary access rather than an assumed leisure preference.
marking_guidance: Context (1): Transport makes the required journey to work feasible.
Reason/conclusion (1): The spending meets necessary access rather than an assumed leisure want.

items.prompt: Explain how preparing for uncertain repair costs can encourage saving when income is sufficient after current needs.
items.canonical_answer: Possible unexpected costs create a need for accessible funds. Setting aside part of current income builds a reserve and can reduce reliance on borrowing if a repair occurs, provided current consumption can be reduced.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): An uncertain repair risk creates a need for a reserve.
Because/mechanism (1): Income can be set aside if current needs permit.
Mechanism development (1): Accumulation creates accessible funds for the repair.
Consequence (1): The reserve can reduce later reliance on borrowing.

items.prompt: Explain the purpose of saving N$200 monthly for twelve months towards an invented N$2,400 purchase, ignoring interest and withdrawals.
items.canonical_answer: The household postpones current consumption to accumulate funds for a planned future purchase. Twelve payments total N$2,400, so borrowing need not finance the target under the stated assumptions.
marking_guidance: Context (1): N$200 over twelve months accumulates N$2,400.
Reason/conclusion (1): Postponed consumption finances the planned purchase without debt under the stated assumptions.

items.prompt: Explain how a loan can bring a purchase forward while reducing future spending capacity, using N$1,000 principal, N$100 total interest, no fees and ten equal repayments.
items.canonical_answer: The loan supplies N$1,000 now so the purchase can occur before funds are saved. Repayment totals N$1,100, or N$110 each time, committing future income and leaving less for other uses during repayment.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): The loan supplies N$1,000 for an immediate purchase.
Because/mechanism (1): Principal plus N$100 interest totals N$1,100.
Mechanism development (1): Ten equal repayments are N$110 each.
Consequence (1): Those commitments leave less future income for other uses.

items.prompt: Explain why higher interest may discourage an optional financed purchase when the borrower’s income and other loan terms are unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Higher interest increases the total repayment cost. The present benefit becomes more expensive relative to waiting or choosing a cheaper purchase, so borrowing may be reduced.
marking_guidance: Context (1): Higher interest raises total repayment cost.
Reason/conclusion (1): Waiting or a cheaper purchase becomes relatively more attractive, so optional borrowing may fall.

items.prompt: Explain a change in saving when household income is unchanged at N$3,000, essentials rise from N$2,400 to N$2,550 for the same quantities and other consumption stays N$450.
items.canonical_answer: The price-related N$150 increase absorbs the former N$150 remainder. With income and other spending unchanged, new saving falls from N$150 to zero; higher essential expenditure does not mean more goods are consumed.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): Essential prices add N$150 without more quantity.
Because/mechanism (1): Income and other spending remain fixed.
Mechanism development (1): The increase absorbs the previous N$150 remainder.
Consequence (1): New saving falls to zero without an increase in real consumption.

items.prompt: Explain why a higher saving return may have a smaller immediate effect on a household with no funds left after essential commitments than on one with a discretionary surplus.
items.canonical_answer: The constrained household cannot readily postpone essential spending to save more. The surplus household has funds it can redirect in response to the return, so its margin for adjustment is larger.
marking_guidance: Context (1): Essential commitments leave one household no discretionary remainder.
Reason/conclusion (1): The surplus household can redirect funds towards saving in response to a higher return.

items.prompt: Invented monthly budgets with no borrowing: A income N$3,000, essentials N$2,400, other consumption N$450, saving N$150; B income N$9,000, essentials N$4,500, other consumption N$2,700, saving N$1,800. Identify two pattern differences (2). Identify two motives for saving (2). Explain why saving shares can differ with income when basic needs absorb much of a smaller budget (2). Identify the spending motive for necessary groceries and the borrowing motive for a loan bridging an urgent repair cost before payday (2).
items.canonical_answer: A has a larger essential share, 80% versus 50%; B has a larger saving share, 20% versus 5%. Emergency reserves and a planned future purchase are saving motives. A smaller budget leaves less after basic needs, limiting saving capacity. Groceries meet current food needs; the repair loan bridges a timing gap in funds.
marking_guidance: Identification, separate points (2): essential share comparison (1), saving share comparison (1). Saving motives (2): emergencies (1), planned purchase (1). Explanation (2): essentials absorb smaller budget (1), less capacity left to save (1). Motives (2): food need (1), timing gap (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented monthly budgets with no borrowing: A income N$3,000, essentials N$2,400, other consumption N$450, saving N$150; B income N$9,000, essentials N$4,500, other consumption N$2,700, saving N$1,800. In the next month, each household’s essential bill rises by N$150 for unchanged quantities. Incomes and other consumption remain unchanged. A saves for emergencies; B saves towards a later purchase. Saving interest becomes more attractive and new borrowing costs rise. Neither has existing debt. Describe three features of the initial saving/spending patterns and motives, each with a distinguishing detail (6). Explain why different saving responses are feasible for A and B, linking their motives and the supplied constraints (7). Discuss whether interest conditions alone explain their changing expenditure patterns (7).
items.canonical_answer: Initially A spends 80% of income on essentials, B saves 20%, and their saving purposes are emergency provision versus a planned purchase. The extra N$150 eliminates A’s saving flow if other spending is maintained, while B can retain N$1,650 saving. A still has its reserve motive but lacks a new-saving remainder; B retains funds to redirect and may respond to attractive returns. Rising loan costs discourage optional borrowing but do not explain the essential-price shock. Interest alone is incomplete; budgets and prices provide direct constraints, while actual optional adjustments depend on preferences.
marking_guidance: Context/data description (6): A essential share (1), 80% detail (1); B saving share (1), 20% detail (1); different saving motives (1), emergency/planned purchase contrast (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): same N$150 shock (1), A’s former saving absorbed (1), A zero new saving (1); B retains N$1,650 (1), so has adjustment capacity (1); A’s motive persists despite constraint (1), B may postpone optional purchase for return (1). Both sides/judgement (7): attractive saving incentive (1), dearer borrowing incentive (1); essential price shock directly alters remainder (1), income differences alter capacity (1); preferences condition response (1); judgement interest alone insufficient (1), tied to supplied budget evidence (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

items.prompt: Invented same-period cases after a saving-rate increase and dearer new loans. Case 1: a lower-income household receives N$3,000 monthly and needs all N$3,000 for essential spending; no existing savings or debt are available. Case 2: a higher-income household receives N$9,000 monthly, uses N$6,000 for current commitments and can choose how to allocate the remainder; it is considering an optional purchase, has no debt and values a future reserve. Prices and incomes are otherwise unchanged. Evaluate whether the lower-income household is likely to raise saving substantially in response to the interest change (7). Evaluate whether the higher-income household is likely to postpone the optional purchase and save more during the same period (7).
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: interest increases the reward to saving, but essentials absorb all income and no stock is available. Substantial new saving is poorly supported unless essential costs can feasibly fall or income changes; dearer borrowing does not create spare income. Case 2: N$3,000 remains after commitments, a valued reserve gives a motive and higher interest strengthens the return to postponing consumption. However, the optional purchase may provide high current satisfaction. More saving is plausible if the future reserve and return outweigh that satisfaction, with the exact response dependent on preferences.
marking_guidance: Case 1 allocation (7): argument for higher return (1), encourages postponement in principle (1); argument against no remainder (1), no existing funds (1); condition feasible budget change needed (1); judgement substantial rise unlikely (1), linked to essentials constraint (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for N$3,000 available (1), reserve/return motive (1); argument against current purchase satisfaction (1), preference uncertainty (1); condition future benefit outweighs present benefit (1); judgement more saving plausible (1), tied to available funds and priority (1). Total marks 14.
